claim: Demand follows the narrowest semantic boundary. Asking for one
semantic product requests only the interfaces and metadata needed for that
product. In particular, checking a caller may read a callee signature but
never the callee body. This is the pipeline-wide consequence of
[Cross-item dependencies stop at semantic interfaces](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#cross-item-dependencies-stop-at-semantic-interfaces).

input change may cause a cheap producer or keyed lookup to execute again.

expensive consumers; the architecture does not claim that every unrelated
edit prevents all upstream execution.

claim: Phase incompleteness is a terminal semantic outcome. A phase
distinguishes a complete result from a conservative result limited by user
error, unsupported functionality, unavailable facts, or an explicit
resource bound. It never presents such a result as computation which merely
needs more scheduling. This is the pipeline-wide consequence of
[Incompleteness is an explicit terminal outcome](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#incompleteness-is-an-explicit-terminal-outcome).

claim: **Speculative checking changes commit atomically.** A candidate or multi-part compatibility check stages its inference changes and obligations in an isolated child version. The whole operation either commits to its direct parent or is discarded; no equality, wake, or obligation from a rejected alternative reaches the requester. The version invariants are defined by [Versioned egraph children are inference transactions](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#versioned-egraph-children-are-inference-transactions).

claim: **Parsing publishes syntax-backed identities, not semantic conclusions.** A represented item has stable local identity, self-contained CST, ordering, ownership, and provenance. Resolution and checking remain downstream operations, and malformed or unsupported top-level syntax is represented explicitly rather than accepted as a definition. Tree-sitter is temporary parser machinery under [Tree-sitter for parsing](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#tree-sitter-for-parsing), not the published identity or syntax representation.

An empty incomplete result is never interpreted as proof that the name or provider does not exist. claim: **Alias normalization preserves reveal context and narrow demand.** An alias retains its identity until an operation requests its value. Revealability participates in the canonical input, and projection normalization reads only the fixed trait, associated item, applicable impl headers, selected associated values, and predicates required for that value. It never reads unrelated impls or bodies. This is the solver consequence of [Named, associated, and opaque aliases share one semantic family](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#named-associated-and-opaque-aliases-share-one-semantic-family) and [Cross-item dependencies stop at semantic interfaces](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#cross-item-dependencies-stop-at-semantic-interfaces).

reviews.reason: Reviewed the complete Stash implementation, newly associated derive copying, and BodyFinalizer in check/finalize.rs. StashCopy recursively reallocates Ptr/Slice contents; generated struct/enum copying visits their fields; BodyFinalizer resolves inference and recursively copies expression, pattern, type, call-substitution and list edges into a fresh target. Release ownership is a caller invariant, as explicitly specified in the architectural-foundations RFD; debug identity/type checks diagnose misuse. All eight ordinary tests were read: compound/slice copying checks actual values; cross-stash tests require debug identity failures or release type mismatch; copied_nested_handles_survive_source_drop_and_destination_growth offsets target layout, drops source, grows storage and checks nested values and sharing. finalized_nested_body_owns_resolved_and_imported_types_after_sources_drop drops both source and imported owners and traverses resolved tuple/child types, spans and sharing. These tests would detect shallow copying. Executed cargo test -p sage-stash --features salsa in debug and release (56 tests each, including UI checks), and the focused sage-ir finalized_nested_body test; all passed.

file/line. A diagnostic is eligible if its primary span intersects the target
line, or if that primary span's macro-expansion ancestry contains an invocation
intersecting it. An empty span matches the line containing its position: for
example, a missing-token diagnostic can point between characters without
covering any character. A position at the start of a line belongs to that line;
EOF belongs to the final source line (including an empty final line after a
trailing newline). The same rule applies to empty invocation spans in expansion
ancestry. Nested expansions retain this ancestry. For Sage, the primary
span is `Diagnostic::span`; entries in `Diagnostic::labels` do not participate

lines; its start alone determines inclusion. Expressions starting on earlier
or later lines are omitted, even if they contain or intersect the target line.
Multiple sibling expressions starting on one line are all included. Each
selected source expression appears once, with its logical filename, expression
kind and readable source description, and completed type. The snapshot omits
line numbers, columns, and ranges. Blocks follow
the same start-line rule; a function-body block starting earlier is not included
merely because it contains the target line.
All type markers contribute to the same snapshot. Files are ordered by logical
path, then marked target lines by source order. Within each target line, output
follows source-tree postorder: children before parents, with siblings in source
order. Repeated markers targeting the same line do not duplicate observations.
Distinct source expressions remain distinct entries even if their rendered text
is identical. Source nesting distinguishes expressions with equal spans.
Generated elaboration nodes do not add duplicate observations, except that
meaningful coercion wrappers are reported after their wrapped expression. Each
wrapper belongs to the selected source expression and exposes its resulting
type, preserving child-before-parent order through a chain of coercions.

source-to-semantic correspondence, fails explicitly. V1 observes expressions;
binding declarations and other semantic entities require future selectors.

claim: The `sage-meta serve <port>` command validates and renders the selected model
before serving its snapshot on the loopback interface. It reports the local
URL and serves until stopped. The port must be an integer from 1 through 65535;
an optional model path selects the input. Invalid arguments, model errors, and
binding failures produce a failing exit status with a diagnostic. Opening the
reported URL provides the specified browser without another serving command.
For example, `cargo run -p sage-meta -- serve 3001` serves the snapshot at
`http://127.0.0.1:3001/`. `cargo run -p sage-meta -- browse` writes a standalone
HTML snapshot. The commands are ways to deliver the browser specified here.

claim: An anchor's full name combines its chapter namespace with the local name
written at its definition. The namespace is derived from the chapter source
path relative to Design, removing the extension and joining path components
with dots. For example, local `point_excerpts` in `design/meta/anchors.md` names
`meta.anchors.point_excerpts`. The same derivation applies to `.sage` chapters.
Section headings, chapter titles, and sidebar ordering do not change these
names; only the source path and local name contribute. Ambiguous
namespace derivations or duplicate full names are errors.
The intended Markdown source spelling is local:
```text
{anchor}`point_excerpts`
A point reference displays its marker line and the next five source lines.
Rust references use the resolved full name, such as
`#[sage::test(meta.anchors.point_excerpts)]` or
// {anchor}`meta.anchors.point_excerpts`. Filename components must normalize to ASCII identifiers; different source
paths that normalize to the same chapter namespace are rejected.

overview of the required changes, with links to the affected Design pages and
anchors. Its implementation plan develops that overview into stages.
Acceptance merges the record and specification changes together; unfinished
implementation or tests remain explicit TODO entries. Subsequent implementation
replaces those entries with code and evidence. Completing an RFD does not require
copying its rules into Design, because the normative changes were already
expressed there.

claim: `.sage` sources reside within the book's configured source directory and each
is rendered as a Design chapter. Design contains a Crates chapter listing the
modeled crates. Each crate has an overview chapter showing its purpose,
dependencies, and modules, with its remaining `.sage` source chapters nested
beneath it. These chapters present the `design/crates/` source tree using the
[architecture browser specified below](#displaying-sage-files). Each source has
one chapter in the shared inventory; rendering does not create a second
canonical copy. Rendering requires no hand-maintained Markdown copies of
`.sage` sources and the built book works without a running Sage server.

without defining specification anchors. Anchors is generated from all active

crate chapters. RFDs record changes and reasoning without defining active
rules. The User's Guide provides non-normative usage instructions.
